title: Connecting the rooks

D0.outcome: Explains that connecting the rooks (all minor pieces out and the queen off the back rank so the rooks see each other) completes development, and why that helps (mutual protection, doubling).

D1.outcome: In a given opening position, lists the pieces and pawns that stand between his rooks and the moves that clear them.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled opening and early-middlegame positions, chooses between connecting the rooks and an attacking move, checking first whether anything hangs.

D3.outcome: Judges when not to hurry (development still incomplete, a tactic intervenes, castling delayed on purpose) and predicts the cost of connecting too early.

misconceptions: Connecting the rooks is a move to make as soon as possible, whatever the position.
sources: docs/first-hours.md 'For Andrew specifically' (remembered Chesscademy basics: castling early, connecting rooks, open files, passed pawns)
sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-45, CI-48 (development takes about seven moves; castling can be delayed)
conditions: Development is otherwise complete and nothing tactical is pending.
Delaying castling can be convenient while forces are deployed.
contrasts: A developing move with tempo is available, so connecting first loses time.
The rooks are connected but both stand on closed files, so the connection has no effect.
An endgame where the rooks were never separated.
